claims.text: Pulumi published a blog post titled "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/.
The post "SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi" provides a closer look at the engine mechanics behind SST's migration to Pulumi.
AWS CDK was SST's (Serverless Stack's) starting point before it had limitations.
AWS CDK ties infrastructure to AWS.
Debugging SST on AWS CDK was frustrating due to CloudFormation templates.
Multi-cloud deployment was nearly impossible with AWS CDK for SST.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster infrastructure experience compared to its prior CDK-based approach.
Pulumi lets SST offer a more flexible infrastructure experience compared to its prior CDK-based approach.
Pulumi lets SST offer a provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
SST was originally built on top of AWS's Cloud Development Kit (CDK).
AWS CDK allows developers to define their infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
With AWS CDK and CloudFormation, the infrastructure code is essentially a code generator that produces an intermediary format such as YAML or JSON.
The intermediary format produced by CDK/CloudFormation is then executed to deploy the resources.
Pulumi treats infrastructure code as a first-class program executed directly during deployment, instead of generating an intermediary format.
AWS CDK supports only AWS as a cloud provider (AWS-only multi-cloud support), while Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-premises infrastructure.
AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi provides real-time debugging.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python as languages, while Pulumi supports any programming language.
AWS CDK deployment speed is slower due to CloudFormation, while Pulumi offers faster direct execution.
AWS CDK has poor visibility that is hard to trace errors with, while Pulumi provides clear deployment state.
AWS CDK's extensibility is limited to the AWS ecosystem, while Pulumi supports custom providers and workflows.
AWS CDK's state management relies on a CloudFormation state file, while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK's secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secret management.
With Pulumi, the infrastructure code is the same code that runs during deployment.
Pulumi's provider-agnostic approach allows the SST team to work with a wide range of cloud and on-premises platforms.
SST's team had to re-implement higher-level components and abstractions that were originally built on top of CDK, when transitioning to Pulumi.

SST's Founding Engineer is quoted as saying: "With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle."
Pulumi provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities as described on the Pulumi Insights product page.
Pulumi provides built-in extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi supports defining infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C#.
Pulumi allows deploying infrastructure across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments from one consistent workflow.
Pulumi offers advanced deployment workflows as documented at https://www.pulumi.com/docs/pulumi-cloud/deployments/.
Pulumi provides better visibility into the deployment process as described on the Pulumi Insights product page.
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies "day one" tasks, as described in Pulumi's AWS guide at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
Pulumi offers an on-demand workshop titled "Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS" at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Pulumi offers upcoming Platform Engineering or DevOps workshops listed at https://www.pulumi.com/resources/#upcoming.
SST is a framework that makes building modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure easy.
SST's Ion is the code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications.
SST Ion's constructs (or components) are deployed using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation (CFN).
Once SST's Ion engine is stable, it will be released as SST v3.
SST leverages Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine.
SST bridges Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST (Serverless Stack) makes money primarily through its managed service called SST Console.
SST Console is optional and includes a free tier.
SST primarily relies on SaaS revenue through its managed platform, with potential supplemental income from enterprise services and consulting.
CDK's AWS-centric nature and CloudFormation became a limitation as SST expanded its focus beyond the AWS ecosystem.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK with an embedded Pulumi engine.
SST v3 bridged Terraform providers.
SST v3 dropped AWS CDK for an embedded Pulumi engine that talks to Terraform-bridged providers.
Running SST v3 requires no Pulumi account.
When SST rebuilt its deployment engine for v3, it did not write a new engine from scratch.
`sst deploy` runs on an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the actual cloud API calls.
SST v3 requires no CDK, no CloudFormation, and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency.
Nitric runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
Defang runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine rather than building its own diff, state, and provider layer from scratch.
SST is still shipping as of this writing.
The SST team's public attention has broadened to include an AI coding agent called opencode.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls.
Running `sst deploy` needs no separate Pulumi install.
Running `sst deploy` needs no Pulumi account.
The Pulumi engine used by SST ships inside the SST CLI.
SST keeps state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account.
The SST team has repeatedly stated, since the Ion rewrite shipped, that SST's architecture is built on the Pulumi engine.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST's team was formerly known as Serverless Stack.
SST lets users define an app's infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file.
SST provides its own components including functions, queues, buckets, and static sites.
Running `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite, code-named Ion, that replaced SST's entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024.
SST v3 (Ion) has been the only supported SST architecture since it shipped in mid-2024.

SST, in its blog post "Moving away from CDK," stated: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST, in its blog post "Moving away from CDK," stated: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
SST's docs, "What is SST," state: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin, in "Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis," wrote: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka, in "SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion," wrote: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`.
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, and Docker builds, among others.
The published `package.json` for SST's platform package depends on a Pulumiverse Vercel provider.
`sst deploy` reads the user's `sst.config.ts` and resolves SST's own components, and this step is SST's responsibility.
SST components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
The Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations.
Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls, via Pulumi's Terraform bridge.
SST writes state to an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account, and this is self-hosted rather than Pulumi Cloud.
SST owns the developer-facing layer: the CLI, the component model, and the local dev loop.
Pulumi's engine owns the provisioning mechanics underneath SST: dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and the plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge is built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's provider ecosystem, adapted for the Pulumi engine, instead of writing and maintaining their own providers.
Pulumi's engine does not require a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service to run.
Pulumi's Automation API works for teams embedding Pulumi programs inside their own tools using the same embeddable-engine approach.
The provider bridge that lets any Pulumi user consume Terraform providers directly is the same bridge used by SST, Nitric, and Defang.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework.
Nitric states in its own docs that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud.
Defang describes its Pulumi provider as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
SST's state lives in the user's own S3 bucket, not in Pulumi's hosted service.
SST does not require a Pulumi account to work.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code.
SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources.
Resources that don't have a dedicated SST construct yet can be defined directly in Pulumi and deployed as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` package on npm is pulling roughly 796,000 downloads a week as of this writing.
SST's own team page credits the same team behind opencode.
opencode is an open source AI coding agent.
opencode has grown quickly since launch.
opencode now carries a larger following on GitHub than SST itself.

Since SST v3 (the Ion rewrite, shipped mid-2024), `sst deploy` runs through an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls, replacing SST's earlier architecture on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
Pulumi's engine is embedded directly in the SST CLI.
SST keeps its own state in an S3 bucket in the user's AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
Users do not need to install Pulumi separately or create a Pulumi account to deploy an SST app.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers, but those providers are bridged through the Pulumi engine rather than run through Terraform itself.
SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.

Users can define resources directly with Pulumi for anything that doesn't yet have a dedicated SST construct, and deploy them as part of the same app, because SST's components compile into Pulumi resource declarations.
SST shipped v4.17.1 in July 2026.
The `sst` package continues to see roughly 796,000 weekly downloads on npm.
The SST team's public attention has broadened to include opencode, an open source AI coding agent, but that hasn't changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.

The `platform/package.json` file in the `anomalyco/sst` repository (formerly `sst/sst`), verified September 2026, lists `@pulumi/pulumi`, `@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, and `@pulumiverse/vercel` as direct dependencies.
The SST repository was formerly named `sst/sst` and is now `anomalyco/sst`.
npm download stats for `sst` show 796,291 downloads for the week of September 5-11, 2026.
The `anomalyco/opencode` GitHub repository's star count was observed in September 2026.
